label: converse
title: Question
body_md:
\label{converse}
Assume that $R$ is quasi-unmixed with infinite residue field, and let
$E_1,E_2\subseteq F$ have finite colength. Does
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]})
=
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)
=
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q)
\]
imply $\overline{E_1}=\overline{E_2}$ in $F$?
head: environment

label: Coro16.5.7SH
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{Coro16.5.7SH}
Suppose that $R$ is formally equidimensional, and let
$E_1\subseteq E_2\subseteq F$ satisfy $\ell_R(F/E_1)<\infty$.
Then $E_1$ is a reduction of $E_2$ in $F$ if and only if
$e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)=e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)$.
head: environment

label: prop:br-degree-polynomiality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:br-degree-polynomiality}
Under the preceding assumptions, there exists a polynomial
$P_E(n;N)\in\mathbb Q[n]$ of degree at most $q$ such that
\[
P_E(n;N)=\ell_R\bigl((S_{en}/E^n)\otimes_RN\bigr)
\qquad(n\gg0).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Give the Veronese algebra $B=S^{(e)}$ its standard grading
$B_n=S_{en}$, and set $T=B\otimes_RN$ and $J=EB$.
Then $T$ is generated in degree zero, and right exactness gives
\[
H(n):=\ell_R\bigl((S_{en}/E^n)\otimes_RN\bigr)
\]
Equip $G=\operatorname{gr}_J(T)$ with the bigrading
\[
G_{i,j}=\frac{E^iT_j}{E^{i+1}T_{j-1}}
\qquad(i,j\geq0),
\]
where $T_{-1}=0$. The algebra $\operatorname{gr}_J(B)$ is generated
over $R$ in bidegrees $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$, and $G$ is finite over it.
Consequently, $K=\bigoplus_{i\geq0,\,j\geq1}G_{i,j}$ is a finite
bigraded submodule.

By \eqref{eq:br-degree-colength}, there is $c\geq1$ with
$\mathfrak m^cT_1\subseteq ET_0$. Since $T_j=B_{j-1}T_1$, this implies
$\mathfrak m^cE^iT_j\subseteq E^{i+1}T_{j-1}$ for $j\geq1$.
Thus $\mathfrak m^cK=0$. Using total degree $i+j$, Hilbert--Serre
shows that $\ell_R(K_n)$ is eventually polynomial. The filtration
\[
T_n\supseteq ET_{n-1}\supseteq\cdots\supseteq E^nT_0
\]
gives $H(n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\ell_R(G_{i,n-i})=\ell_R(K_n)$,
proving polynomiality.

Iterating $\mathfrak m^cT_1\subseteq ET_0$ yields
$\mathfrak m^{cn}T_n\subseteq E^nT_0$. Therefore
\[
H(n)\leq\ell_R(T_n/\mathfrak m^{cn}T_n)
 =\binom{en+p-1}{p-1}\ell_R(N/\mathfrak m^{cn}N).
\]
Since $\dim_RN=d$, one has
$\ell_R(N/\mathfrak m^{cn}N)=O(n^d)$, while
$\binom{en+p-1}{p-1}=O(n^{p-1})$. Hence $H(n)=O(n^q)$,
which proves the degree bound.
which proves the degree bound.
head: environment

label: def:br-degree
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:br-degree}
The Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicity of $E$ in degree $e$, with
coefficients in $N$ and relative to $S$, is defined by
\[
\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E;N)
:=q!\lim_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\ell_R((S_{en}/E^n)\otimes_RN)}{n^q}.
\]
When $N=R$, we omit $N$
from the notation.
head: environment

label: rem:br-degree-conventions
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:br-degree-conventions}
The number $\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E;N)$ is a nonnegative integer:
$P_E(n;N)$ is eventually integer-valued and nonnegative, so its
normalized coefficient in degree $q$ is integral and nonnegative.
It may vanish; for example, it vanishes when $E=S_e$.
For $e=1$, the definition is the classical Buchsbaum--Rim
multiplicity $e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E;N)$. For $e>1$, it is relative to
multiplication in $S$, and must not be confused with the classical
multiplicity of the inclusion into the free module $S_e$, whose
ambient symmetric algebra would instead be
$\operatorname{Sym}_R(S_e)$.
head: environment

label: lem:br-degree-fiber-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:br-degree-fiber-bound}
Let $(A,\mathfrak n)$ be a Noetherian local ring of dimension
$\delta\geq1$, let $C=A[t_1,\ldots,t_p]$, and let $U\subseteq C_e$
have finite colength, where $e\geq1$. Grade $\mathcal A=A[U]$ by
assigning degree one to $U$. Then
\[
\dim(\mathcal A/\mathfrak n\mathcal A)\leq\delta+p-1.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to consider the images of $\mathcal A$ over the minimal
prime quotients of $A$. Indeed, the kernel of the map to the product
of these images is nilpotent, and the resulting finitely many
closed subsets cover $\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal A)$.

Suppose first that $A$ is a domain of positive dimension
$\delta'$. On $X=\mathbb P_A^{p-1}$, the forms in $U$ define a
linear system which is the complete degree-$e$ system outside the
closed fiber. Its graph closure $Y$ is the blowup of its base ideal.
It is integral, has dimension $\delta'+p-1$, and maps properly and
surjectively to $\operatorname{Proj}(A[U])$. Surjectivity follows
because its generic image is dense and the morphism is proper.
The closed fiber $Y_{\mathfrak n}$ is a proper closed subset of $Y$,
so its dimension is at most $\delta'+p-2$. Surjectivity on closed
fibers now gives
$\dim(A[U]/\mathfrak nA[U])\leq\delta'+p-1$.
If the domain quotient has dimension zero, it is a field, and its
algebra of forms has dimension at most $p$. Both bounds are at most
$\delta+p-1$.
head: environment

label: lem:br-degree-shift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:br-degree-shift}
With $B=S^{(e)}$, $T=B\otimes_RN$, and $H(n)=\ell_R(T_n/E^nT_0)$,
for every fixed integer $h\geq1$ one has
\[
\ell_R(T_{n+h}/E^nT_h)=H(n+h)+O(n^{q-1}).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $R'=R/\operatorname{Ann}_R(N)$ and let $E'$ be the image of $E$
in $S_e\otimes_RR'$. The module
$(S_e\otimes_RR')/E'$ has finite length: outside the closed point
its tensor product with the nonzero localized module $N$ vanishes,
so Nakayama's lemma forces it to vanish. Also $\dim R'=d$.
Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:br-degree-fiber-bound}, applied to
$\mathcal A=R'[E']$, gives
$\dim(\mathcal A/\mathfrak m\mathcal A)\leq q$.

For fixed $h$, the graded module
\[
V_h=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\frac{E^nT_h}{E^{n+h}T_0}
\]
is finite over $\mathcal A$, since its numerator is generated by
$T_h$ in degree zero. Choose $c$ as in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:br-degree-polynomiality}. Then
$\mathfrak m^{ch}T_h\subseteq E^hT_0$, whence
$\mathfrak m^{ch}V_h=0$ and $\dim_{\mathcal A}V_h\leq q$.
Hilbert--Serre yields
$\ell_R((V_h)_n)=O(n^{q-1})$.
The assertion follows from the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow\frac{E^nT_h}{E^{n+h}T_0}
\longrightarrow\frac{T_{n+h}}{E^{n+h}T_0}
\longrightarrow\frac{T_{n+h}}{E^nT_h}
\longrightarrow0.
\]
head: environment

label: prop:br-degree-KT-identification
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:br-degree-KT-identification}
Under the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:br-degree-polynomiality},
one has
\[
\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E;N)=e^{q,0}(E;N),
\]
Here $e^{q,0}(E;N)$ is the Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicity of
Kleiman--Thorup \cite[Section~8]{Kleiman-Thorup2}, computed for
$S\otimes_RN$ and the degree-$e$ submodule $E$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Condition~\eqref{eq:br-degree-colength} implies that the base locus
of $E$ on $\operatorname{Proj}(S)$ meets the support of
$\widetilde{S\otimes_RN}$ only in the closed fiber. Hence
\cite[Proposition~8.2]{Kleiman-Thorup2} applies to
\[
\lambda(n,b)=\ell_R\left(
\frac{S_{en+b}\otimes_RN}{E^n(S_b\otimes_RN)}\right).
\]
For $n,b\gg0$, this is a polynomial of total degree at most $q$,
whose homogeneous component of degree $q$ is
\[
\sum_{i+k=q}\frac{e^{i,k}(E;N)}{i!\,k!}n^ib^k.
\]
Choose a fixed $h\geq1$ sufficiently large that $b=eh$ belongs to
the polynomial range. Then
\[
\lambda(n,eh)=\frac{e^{q,0}(E;N)}{q!}n^q+O(n^{q-1}).
\]
On the other hand, Lemma~\ref{lem:br-degree-shift} gives
\[
\lambda(n,eh)=H(n+h)+O(n^{q-1})
\]
Comparison proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: rem:br-degree-specialization
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:br-degree-specialization}
The preceding argument does not specialize the polynomial identity
of \cite[Proposition~8.2]{Kleiman-Thorup2} at $b=0$, which need not
lie in its stated range of validity. Instead, it fixes a sufficiently
large value $b=eh$ and uses Lemma~\ref{lem:br-degree-shift} to compare
the leading coefficients.
head: environment

label: remark1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{remark1}
Let $M\subseteq F$ have finite colength, and let $r\geq1$.
Regard $M^r$ as a submodule of $S_r$. Since
$(M^r)^n=M^{rn}$ inside $S_{rn}$, the defining Hilbert functions
satisfy
\[
\ell_R\!\left((S_{rn}/(M^r)^n)\otimes_RN\right)
=\ell_R\!\left((S_{rn}/M^{rn})\otimes_RN\right).
\]
The leading term on the right is
$\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(M;N)(rn)^q/q!$.
Consequently,
\[
\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(M^r;N)
=r^q\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(M;N).
\]
In particular, for $N=R$,
$\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(M^r)=r^{d+p-1}e_{\mathrm{BR}}(M)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Combining \cite[Proposition~8.2]{Kleiman-Thorup2} with
multigraded Hilbert--Serre yields a polynomial in
$\mathbb Q[n_1,n_2]$ that agrees with $h_R(n_1,n_2;N)$
for $n_1,n_2\gg0$.
Indeed, one applies these results to the two outer terms of
the exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow
\frac{E_2^{n_2}T_{n_1}}{E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0}
\longrightarrow
\frac{T_{n_1+n_2}}{E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0}
\longrightarrow
\frac{T_{n_1+n_2}}{E_2^{n_2}T_{n_1}}
\longrightarrow0,
\]
where $T=S\otimes_RN$, using the associated graded filtration
induced by $E_1$ for the left-hand term.
Moreover, choosing $c\geq1$ with
$\mathfrak m^cF\subseteq E_1\cap E_2$ and setting $u=n_1+n_2$,
we obtain
\[
0 \leq h_R(n_1,n_2;N)
\leq
\binom{u+p-1}{p-1}\ell_R(N/\mathfrak m^{cu}N)
\]
Since eventual polynomiality has already been established, this
uniform estimate bounds the total degree by $d+p-1$.
head: environment

label: prop:mixed-br-arbitrary-degree
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:mixed-br-arbitrary-degree}
Fix positive integers $e_1,e_2$, and let
$E_i\subseteq S_{e_i}=F^{e_i}$ be submodules satisfying
$\ell_R(S_{e_i}/E_i)<\infty$ for $i=1,2$. Then the function
\[
h_R(n_1,n_2;N) = \ell_R\left( \left( S_{e_1n_1+e_2n_2}/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2} \right)\otimes_RN \right)
\]
agrees, for $n_1,n_2\gg0$, with a polynomial in $\mathbb Q[n_1,n_2]$ of total degree at most $q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $T=S\otimes_RN$, $T_v=S_v\otimes_RN$. All products acting on $T$ are understood as the images of the corresponding multiplication maps. By right exactness of tensor products, $\left( S_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2} \right)\otimes_RN \cong T_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0$, where $u=e_1n_1+e_2n_2$.

Since $E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0 \subseteq E_2^{n_2}T_{e_1n_1} \subseteq T_u$, we obtain an exact sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow \frac{E_2^{n_2}T_{e_1n_1}}{E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0} \longrightarrow \frac{T_u}{E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0} \longrightarrow \frac{T_u}{E_2^{n_2}T_{e_1n_1}} \longrightarrow 0.
\]
Consequently, $h_R(n_1,n_2;N)=A(n_1,n_2)+B(n_1,n_2)$, where $A(n_1,n_2)$ and $B(n_1,n_2)$ denote the lengths of the left-hand and right-hand terms, respectively.

We first consider $B(n_1,n_2)$. Since $\ell_R(S_{e_2}/E_2)<\infty$, the hypotheses of \cite[Proposition~8.2]{Kleiman-Thorup2} are satisfied. Hence there exists a polynomial $Q(a,b)\in\mathbb Q[a,b]$ such that $\ell_R\left( T_{e_2a+b}/E_2^aT_b \right) = Q(a,b)$ for $a,b\gg0$. Taking $a=n_2$ and $b=e_1n_1$, we obtain $B(n_1,n_2)=Q(n_2,e_1n_1)$ for $n_1,n_2\gg0$. Thus $B$ is eventually polynomial in $n_1,n_2$.

We now prove the eventual polynomiality of $A$. Consider the externally bigraded algebra and module $\mathcal C = \bigoplus_{j,b\geq0}E_2^bS_{e_1j}$ and $\mathcal T = \bigoplus_{j,b\geq0}E_2^bT_{e_1j}$, where the summand $E_2^bS_{e_1j}$ has bidegree $(j,b)$.

Since $S_{e_1j}=(S_{e_1})^j$, the algebra $\mathcal C$ is generated over $R$ by its components of degrees $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. Moreover, $\mathcal T$ is a finite graded $\mathcal C$-module generated by $\mathcal T_{0,0}=T_0=N$.

Let $\mathcal J$ be the ideal of $\mathcal C$ generated by $E_1$ in bidegree $(1,0)$. Set $\mathcal A=\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal J}(\mathcal C)$ and $G=\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal J}(\mathcal T)$. Then $G$ is a finite graded module over the Noetherian algebra $\mathcal A$.

Combining the associated grading with the original bigrading, and writing $j$ for the residual first degree after removing the $\mathcal J$-filtration degree, we obtain
\[
G_{i,j,b} = \frac{ E_1^iE_2^bT_{e_1j} }{ E_1^{i+1}E_2^bT_{e_1(j-1)} }, \qquad i,j,b\geq0,
\]
where the denominator is understood to be zero when $j=0$.

The generators of $\mathcal A$ have tridegrees $(1,0,0)$, $(0,1,0)$, and $(0,0,1)$. The submodule
\[
K=\bigoplus_{i,b\geq0,\,j\geq1}G_{i,j,b}
\]
is stable under the action of $\mathcal A$, and hence is finite over $\mathcal A$.

Choose $c\geq1$ such that $\mathfrak m^cS_{e_1}\subseteq E_1$. For $j\geq1$, the equality $T_{e_1j}=S_{e_1}T_{e_1(j-1)}$ implies $\mathfrak m^cE_1^iE_2^bT_{e_1j} \subseteq E_1^{i+1}E_2^bT_{e_1(j-1)}$. Thus $\mathfrak m^cK=0$.

Now replace the trigrading by the bigrading $(i,j,b)\longmapsto(i+j,b)$. Under this regrading, $\mathcal A$ becomes a standard bigraded algebra generated in degrees $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. Therefore $K$ is a finite bigraded module over $\mathcal A/\mathfrak m^c\mathcal A$, whose degree-zero component is the Artinian ring $R/\mathfrak m^c$.

The multigraded Hilbert--Serre theorem gives a polynomial
$P_K(X,Y)\in\mathbb Q[X,Y]$ such that
\[
\ell_R(K_{n_1,n_2})=P_K(n_1,n_2)
\qquad(n_1,n_2\gg0).
\]

By the definition of the regrading, $K_{n_1,n_2} = \bigoplus_{i=0}^{n_1-1} G_{i,n_1-i,n_2}$. The filtration $$E_2^{n_2}T_{e_1n_1} \supseteq E_1E_2^{n_2}T_{e_1(n_1-1)} \supseteq\cdots\supseteq E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0$$ has successive quotients $G_{i,n_1-i,n_2}$ for $0\leq i\leq n_1-1$. Therefore,
\[
A(n_1,n_2) = \sum_{i=0}^{n_1-1} \ell_R\left(G_{i,n_1-i,n_2}\right) = \ell_R(K_{n_1,n_2}) = P_K(n_1,n_2)
\]
for $n_1,n_2\gg0$. Hence $h_R(n_1,n_2;N) = P_K(n_1,n_2)+Q(n_2,e_1n_1)$ for all sufficiently large $n_1,n_2$. Thus $h_R$ agrees eventually with a polynomial $P(n_1,n_2)\in\mathbb Q[n_1,n_2]$.

It remains to bound the total degree of $P$. Choose $c\geq1$ such that $\mathfrak m^cS_{e_i}\subseteq E_i$ ($i=1,2$). Since $S$ is a polynomial ring, $(S_{e_1})^{n_1}(S_{e_2})^{n_2}=S_u$ for $u=e_1n_1+e_2n_2$. Consequently, $\mathfrak m^{c(n_1+n_2)}T_u \subseteq E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0$. Since $T_u\cong N^{\binom{u+p-1}{p-1}}$ as an $R$-module, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
0\leq h_R(n_1,n_2;N)
&\leq \ell_R\!\left(T_u/\mathfrak m^{c(n_1+n_2)}T_u\right)\\
&=\binom{u+p-1}{p-1}
\ell_R\!\left(N/\mathfrak m^{c(n_1+n_2)}N\right)\\
&=O\!\left((n_1+n_2)^q\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose that $P$ had total degree $D>q$, and let $P_D$ denote its homogeneous component of degree $D$. Since $P_D\neq0$, there exist positive integers $a,b$ such that $P_D(a,b)\neq0$. Hence $P(an,bn) = P_D(a,b)n^D+O(n^{D-1})$, which contradicts the estimate $P(an,bn)=O(n^q)$. Therefore, $\deg P\leq q=d+p-1$. This proves the proposition.

label: notation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{notation}
For $u=e_1n_1+e_2n_2$, right exactness gives the natural
isomorphism
\[
(S_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2})\otimes_RN
\cong
\frac{S_u\otimes_RN}
{\operatorname{Im}\!\left(
E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}\otimes_RN
\longrightarrow S_u\otimes_RN
\right)}.
\]
Thus, with $T=S\otimes_RN$, the function above is precisely
$\ell_R(T_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}T_0)$.
No injectivity of the tensor-induced map is assumed.

label: rem:comparison-graded-notation
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:comparison-graded-notation}
The degree-one conventions above agree with the graded formulation
in \cite[Remark~2.1 and Section~4]{Bedregal-Perez}.
Indeed, take $G=S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$ and
\[
M=S\otimes_RN
=\bigoplus_{v\geq0}M_v
=\bigoplus_{v\geq0}(F^v\otimes_RN),
\]
which has dimension $d+p$. If $E\subseteq F$ and
$\mathcal R(E)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}\mathcal R_n(E)$ is its Rees
algebra, then $\mathcal R_n(E)=E^n$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_R\!\left(M_n/\mathcal R_n(E)M_0\right)
&=\ell_R\!\left(
\frac{F^n\otimes_RN}
{\operatorname{Im}(E^n\otimes_RN\longrightarrow F^n\otimes_RN)}
\right)\\
&=\ell_R\!\left((F^n/E^n)\otimes_RN\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Likewise, for $E_i\subseteq S_{e_i}$ and $u=e_1n_1+e_2n_2$,
the graded-module expression $\ell_R(M_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}M_0)$ equals
\(
\ell_R\!\left(
\left(S_u/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}\right)\otimes_RN
\right),
\)
as explained in Remark~\ref{notation}.

label: lem:mixed-product-formula
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$.
First, $E_1E_2$ has finite colength in $S_2$:
if $\mathfrak m^cF\subseteq E_1\cap E_2$, then
$\mathfrak m^{2c}S_2\subseteq E_1E_2$.
Thus $\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1E_2;N)$ is defined.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:mixed-br-arbitrary-degree}, for
$n_1,n_2\gg0$ one has
\[
\ell_R\!\left(
(S_{n_1+n_2}/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2})\otimes_RN
\right)
=
\sum_{i=0}^{q}
\frac{e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)}
{(q-i)!\,i!}\,
n_1^{q-i}n_2^i
+P_{<q}(n_1,n_2),
\]
where $P_{<q}$ has total degree less than $q$.
Taking $n_1=n_2=n$ yields
\begin{equation}\label{formula0}
\ell_R\!\left(
(S_{2n}/E_1^nE_2^n)\otimes_RN
\right)
=
\frac{n^q}{q!}
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)
+O(n^{q-1}).
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the definition of multiplicity in
degree two gives
\begin{equation}\label{formula1}
\ell_R\!\left(
(S_{2n}/(E_1E_2)^n)\otimes_RN
\right)
=
\frac{\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1E_2;N)}{q!}\,n^q
+O(n^{q-1}).
\end{equation}
Since $(E_1E_2)^n=E_1^nE_2^n$ inside $S$, the left-hand
sides of \eqref{formula0} and \eqref{formula1} agree.
Comparing the coefficients of $n^q$ proves the formula.

label: mixed
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{mixed}
Fix positive integers $e_1,e_2$, and let
$E_i\subseteq S_{e_i}=\operatorname{Sym}_R^{e_i}(F)$ have finite
colength for $i=1,2$. Then, for all positive integers $r,s$,
\begin{equation}\label{formula}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^rE_2^s;N)
=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N\right)
 r^{q-i}s^i.
\end{equation}
When $e_1=e_2=1$, this becomes
\begin{equation}\label{formula2}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^rE_2^s;N)
=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
 e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N\right)
 r^{q-i}s^i.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Mixed product formula in arbitrary degrees

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the eventual mixed Hilbert polynomial as $P(X,Y)$. Its
homogeneous component of degree $q$ is
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\frac{\widetilde e_{\rm BR}
(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)}{(q-i)!\,i!}X^{q-i}Y^i.
\]
For fixed positive integers $r,s$, substituting $(X,Y)=(rn,sn)$
shows that the leading coefficient of $P(rn,sn)$ is
\[
\frac{1}{q!}\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)r^{q-i}s^i.
\]
The same function is the Hilbert function defining
$\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^rE_2^s;N)$, since
$(E_1^rE_2^s)^n=E_1^{rn}E_2^{sn}$. Comparing leading coefficients
proves \eqref{formula}. If $e_1=e_2=1$, the arbitrary-degree
coefficients are the ordinary mixed Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities,
which gives \eqref{formula2}.
head: environment

label: cor:ideal-product
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:ideal-product}
Let $I,J$ be $\mathfrak m$-primary ideals of $R$. In the special case
$p=1$ (so that $F=R$ and $q=d$), the preceding formula becomes
\[
e(I^rJ^s;N)=
\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom di
e\left(I^{[d-i]},J^{[i]};N\right)r^{d-i}s^i
\qquad(r,s\geq0).
\]
In particular,
\[
e(IJ;N)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom di
e\left(I^{[d-i]},J^{[i]};N\right).
\]
head: environment
name: Product formula for ideals

title: Proof
body_md:
When $p=1$, $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(R)=R[t]$ and each graded
component $S_n$ is a free $R$-module of rank one.  Thus the
Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities and the mixed Buchsbaum--Rim
multiplicities specialize to the usual Hilbert--Samuel mixed
multiplicities of $I$ and $J$.  The identities follow from
\eqref{formula2}.
head: environment

label: lem:mixed-br-basic-properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mixed-br-basic-properties}

\begin{enumerate}
\item For finite-colength submodules $E_1,E_2\subseteq F$ and
positive integers $u,v$, regard $E_1^u$ and $E_2^v$ as submodules of
$S_u$ and $S_v$, respectively. Then, for $0\leq i\leq q$,
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}\!\left((E_1^u)^{[q-i]},(E_2^v)^{[i]}\right)
=u^{q-i}v^i e_{\rm BR}\!\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right).
\]
\item For every finite-colength submodule $E\subseteq F$ and
$0\leq i\leq q$,
\[
e_{\rm BR}\!\left(E^{[q-i]},E^{[i]}\right)=e_{\rm BR}(E).
\]
\item If $K_1\subseteq M_1$ and $K_2\subseteq M_2$ are
finite-colength submodules of $F$, with $K_j$ a reduction of $M_j$
for $j=1,2$, then
\[
e_{\rm BR}\!\left(K_1^{[q-i]},K_2^{[i]}\right)
=e_{\rm BR}\!\left(M_1^{[q-i]},M_2^{[i]}\right)
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q).
\]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(i)}
For every pair of positive integers $r,s$, Corollary~\ref{mixed}
and the identity
$(E_1^u)^r(E_2^v)^s=E_1^{ur}E_2^{vs}$ give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom{q}{i}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}
\left((E_1^u)^{[q-i]},(E_2^v)^{[i]}\right)
r^{q-i}s^i&= \widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{ur}E_2^{vs})\\
=&
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
u^{q-i}v^i r^{q-i}s^i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since this equality holds for all positive integers $r,s$,
it is a polynomial identity. Comparing coefficients of
$r^{q-i}s^i$ proves \textup{(i)}.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(ii)}
By Corollary~\ref{mixed} and Remark~\ref{remark1},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_1^{[i]}\right)
r^{q-i}s^i
&=\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{r+s})\\
&=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)(r+s)^q\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)r^{q-i}s^i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing coefficients proves \textup{(ii)}.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(iii)}
We first establish reduction invariance for multiplicities
in arbitrary degree. Let $A\subseteq B\subseteq S_e$ have
finite colength, and suppose that $A$ is a reduction of $B$.
Choose $h\geq1$ such that
\(
B^n=A^{n-h}B^h
\,\,(n\geq h).
\)
Since $A^n\subseteq B^n\subseteq A^{n-h}S_{eh}$, we obtain
\[
\ell_R(S_{en}/A^{n-h}S_{eh})
\leq
\ell_R(S_{en}/B^n)
\leq
\ell_R(S_{en}/A^n).
\]
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:br-degree-shift} to $A$, with
coefficient module $R$ and index $n-h$, gives
\[
\ell_R(S_{en}/A^{n-h}S_{eh})
=
\ell_R(S_{en}/A^n)+O(n^{q-1}).
\]
Thus the two outer terms have the same normalized leading
coefficient. Dividing by $n^q/q!$ and taking limits yields
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(A)=\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(B).
\]

Now fix positive integers $r,s$. Since $K_1$ is a reduction
of $M_1$ and $K_2$ is a reduction of $M_2$, for $n\gg0$ we have
\[
M_1^{r(n+1)}=K_1^rM_1^{rn},
\qquad
M_2^{s(n+1)}=K_2^sM_2^{sn}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
(M_1^rM_2^s)^{n+1}
=(K_1^rK_2^s)(M_1^rM_2^s)^n.
\]
Hence $K_1^rK_2^s$ is a reduction of $M_1^rM_2^s$, both
regarded as submodules of $S_{r+s}$.

These modules have finite colength: choosing $a,b\geq1$
with $\mathfrak m^aF\subseteq K_1$ and
$\mathfrak m^bF\subseteq K_2$, we have
\[
\mathfrak m^{ar+bs}S_{r+s}
\subseteq K_1^rK_2^s
\subseteq M_1^rM_2^s.
\]
The reduction invariance proved above therefore gives
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(K_1^rK_2^s)
=\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(M_1^rM_2^s).
\]
By Corollary~\ref{mixed}, this equality becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(K_1^{[q-i]},K_2^{[i]}\right)r^{q-i}s^i=
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(M_1^{[q-i]},M_2^{[i]}\right)r^{q-i}s^i.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since it holds for all positive integers $r,s$, comparison
of coefficients proves \textup{(iii)}.

label: ex:mixed-br-teissier-failure
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:mixed-br-teissier-failure}
{\rm The classical quadratic Teissier inequality does not extend
to mixed Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities under the finite-colength
hypothesis alone.

Let $R=k[[x]]$, let $F=R^2$, and set $E_1=xF$ and $E_2=x^2F$.
Then $d+p-1=2$. For $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$, one has
\[
E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}
=x^{n_1+2n_2}S_{n_1+n_2},
\]
and consequently
\[
\ell_R(S_{n_1+n_2}/E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2})
=(n_1+2n_2)(n_1+n_2+1).
\]
Comparing the quadratic terms gives
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)=2,\qquad
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)=4,\qquad
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[1]})=3.
\]
Hence
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[1]})^2
=9>8
=e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2).
\]}
head: environment

label: ex:failure-teissier-modules
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:failure-teissier-modules}
{\rm The direct analogue of Teissier's inequality fails for mixed
Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities, even over a regular local ring.

Let $R=k[[x,y,z]]$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(x,y,z)$,
and let $F=R^2$ and $N=R$. Set
\[
E_1=\mathfrak mF,\qquad E_2=\mathfrak m^2F.
\]
Both modules have finite colength in $F$, and
$q=\dim R+\operatorname{rank}F-1=4$.
Writing $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$, we have
\[
E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}
=\mathfrak m^{n_1+2n_2}S_{n_1+n_2}.
\]
Since $S_{n_1+n_2}$ is free of rank $n_1+n_2+1$ and
$\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^t)=\binom{t+2}{3}$, it follows that
\[
h_R(n_1,n_2;R)
=(n_1+n_2+1)\binom{n_1+2n_2+2}{3}.
\]
Its homogeneous component of total degree four is
\[
\frac{(n_1+n_2)(n_1+2n_2)^3}{6}
=
\frac{
n_1^4+7n_1^3n_2+18n_1^2n_2^2
+20n_1n_2^3+8n_2^4
}{6}.
\]
Comparing this expression with
\(
\sum_{i=0}^{4}
\frac{
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[4-i]},E_2^{[i]})
}{(4-i)!\,i!}\,
n_1^{4-i}n_2^i,
\)
we obtain
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)=4,\qquad
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)=32,\qquad
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[3]},E_2^{[1]})=7.
\]
Consequently,
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[3]},E_2^{[1]})^4
=7^4=2401
>
2048=4^3\cdot32
=e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)^3e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2).
\]
Thus the inequality
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]})^q
\leq
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)^{q-i}e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)^i
\]
does not hold in general for submodules of finite colength.}
head: environment

label: ex:diagonal-modules-teissier-failure
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:diagonal-modules-teissier-failure}
{\rm The analogue of Teissier's inequality fails even for diagonal
modules defined by distinct integrally closed primary ideals
over a two-dimensional regular local ring.

Let $R=k[[x,y]]$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(x,y)$,
and let $F=Rf_1\oplus Rf_2$. Set
\[
E_1=\mathfrak m f_1\oplus\mathfrak m^2f_2,
\qquad
E_2=\mathfrak m^3f_1\oplus\mathfrak m^4f_2.
\]
The four coordinate ideals are distinct, integrally closed,
and $\mathfrak m$-primary. Moreover,
$q=\dim R+\operatorname{rank}F-1=3$.

Identify $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$ with $R[t_1,t_2]$.
For $0\leq k\leq n_1+n_2$, the coefficient ideal of
$t_1^kt_2^{n_1+n_2-k}$ in $E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}$ is
$\mathfrak m^{2n_1+4n_2-k}$. Indeed, every admissible
decomposition $k=i+j$ contributes the ideal
\[
\mathfrak m^{i+2(n_1-i)+3j+4(n_2-j)}
=\mathfrak m^{2n_1+4n_2-k}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
h_R(n_1,n_2;R)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n_1+n_2}
\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^{2n_1+4n_2-k})
=
\sum_{k=0}^{n_1+n_2}
\binom{2n_1+4n_2-k+1}{2}.
\]
Its homogeneous component of total degree three is
\[
\frac{(2n_1+4n_2)^3-(n_1+3n_2)^3}{6}
=
\frac{
7n_1^3+39n_1^2n_2+69n_1n_2^2+37n_2^3
}{6}.
\]
Comparing coefficients with
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{3}
\frac{e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[3-i]},E_2^{[i]})}
{(3-i)!\,i!}\,n_1^{3-i}n_2^i,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)&=7,
&
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)&=37,\\
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[2]},E_2^{[1]})&=13,
&
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[2]})&=23.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both inequalities fail:
\[
13^3=2197>1813=7^2\cdot37,
\qquad
23^3=12167>9583=7\cdot37^2.
\]
In particular, requiring the coordinate ideals to be distinct
and integrally closed does not suffice to guarantee
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]})^q
\leq
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)^{q-i}e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)^i.
\]}

label: ex:non-diagonal-teissier-failure
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:non-diagonal-teissier-failure}
{\rm The analogue of Teissier's inequality also fails for
finite-colength submodules that cannot be diagonalized
by a change of basis of the ambient free module.

Let $R=k[[x,y]]$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(x,y)$,
let $F=Rf_1\oplus Rf_2$, and take $N=R$. Consider
\[
E_1=
\operatorname{Im}
\begin{pmatrix}
x&y&0\\
0&x&y
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
E_2=
\operatorname{Im}
\begin{pmatrix}
x^2&y^2&0\\
0&x^2&y^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their maximal-minor ideals are
$(x^2,xy,y^2)$ and $(x^4,x^2y^2,y^4)$, respectively.
Both are $\mathfrak m$-primary, so
$\ell_R(F/E_j)<\infty$ for $j=1,2$.

Each module has exactly three minimal generators.
Indeed, the displayed generators have linearly independent
initial forms in degrees one and two, respectively.
Moreover, $E_j\subseteq\mathfrak mF$.
If either module were diagonal in some basis of $F$, its
two coordinate ideals would therefore be proper
$\mathfrak m$-primary ideals. Each would require at least
two generators, contradicting $\mu_R(E_j)=3$.
Thus neither module is diagonalizable.

We next determine their reductions. For elements $a,b\in R$,
write
\[
M=(a,b)F,\qquad
E=R(af_1)+R(bf_1+af_2)+R(bf_2).
\]
Inside $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)=R[t_1,t_2]$, put
\(
A=at_1,\,\, B=bt_1,\,\, C=at_2,\,\, D=bt_2.
\)
Then $M$ is generated by $A,B,C,D$, whereas $E$ is
generated by $A,B+C,D$. Since $BC=AD$, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
BC&\in EM,\\
B^2&=B(B+C)-AD\in EM,\\
C^2&=C(B+C)-AD\in EM.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every remaining quadratic product of the generators
contains $A$ or $D$. Hence $M^2=EM$, proving that
$E$ is a reduction of $M$.

Applying this observation with $(a,b)=(x,y)$ shows that
$E_1$ is a reduction of $\mathfrak mF$.
With $(a,b)=(x^2,y^2)$, it shows that $E_2$ is a reduction
of $(x^2,y^2)F$.
Furthermore,
\[
(\mathfrak m^2)^2=(x^2,y^2)\mathfrak m^2,
\]
so $(x^2,y^2)F$ is a reduction of $\mathfrak m^2F$.
By transitivity, $E_2$ is a reduction of $\mathfrak m^2F$.

By invariance of mixed Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities under
reductions in each argument, it remains to compute the
multiplicities of $\mathfrak mF$ and $\mathfrak m^2F$.
Their length function is
\[
\ell_R\!\left(
S_{n_1+n_2}/
(\mathfrak mF)^{n_1}(\mathfrak m^2F)^{n_2}
\right)
=
(n_1+n_2+1)\binom{n_1+2n_2+1}{2}.
\]
Its homogeneous component of degree three is
\[
\frac{(n_1+n_2)(n_1+2n_2)^2}{2}
=
\frac{n_1^3+5n_1^2n_2+8n_1n_2^2+4n_2^3}{2}.
\]
Comparing normalized coefficients yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)&=3,
&
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)&=12,\\
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[2]},E_2^{[1]})&=5,
&
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[2]})&=8.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $q=\dim R+\operatorname{rank}F-1=3$, both proposed
inequalities fail:
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[2]},E_2^{[1]})^3
=125>108
=e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)^2e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2),
\]
and
\[
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[2]})^3
=512>432
=e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1)e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_2)^2.
\]}

label: ex:failure-log-convexity-dim-three
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:failure-log-convexity-dim-three}
{\rm Mixed Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities need not satisfy the
Teissier log-convexity inequalities, even over a regular local
ring of dimension three.

Let $R=k[[x,y,z]]$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(x,y,z)$,
and set $F=R^2$, $N=R$, $E_1=\mathfrak mF$, and
$E_2=\mathfrak m^2F$. Both modules have finite colength in $F$.
Here $d=3$, $p=2$, and $q=d+p-1=4$.

Writing $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)=R[t_1,t_2]$, we have
\[
E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}
=\mathfrak m^{n_1+2n_2}S_{n_1+n_2}.
\]
Since $S_{n_1+n_2}$ is free of rank $n_1+n_2+1$ and
$\ell_R(R/\mathfrak m^a)=\binom{a+2}{3}$, it follows that
\[
h_R(n_1,n_2;R)
=
\ell_R\left(
\frac{S_{n_1+n_2}}{E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}}
\right)
=
(n_1+n_2+1)\binom{n_1+2n_2+2}{3}.
\]
Its homogeneous component of degree four is
\[
\begin{aligned}
[h_R]_4
&=\frac{(n_1+n_2)(n_1+2n_2)^3}{6}\\
&=\frac{
n_1^4+7n_1^3n_2+18n_1^2n_2^2
+20n_1n_2^3+8n_2^4}{6}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Set
\[
c_i=e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[4-i]},E_2^{[i]};R\right),
\qquad 0\leq i\leq4.
\]
By definition,
\[
[h_R]_4
=\sum_{i=0}^4\frac{c_i}{(4-i)!\,i!}n_1^{4-i}n_2^i.
\]
Comparing coefficients gives
\[
(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)=(4,7,12,20,32).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1^2&=49>48=c_0c_2,\\
c_2^2&=144>140=c_1c_3,\\
c_3^2&=400>384=c_2c_4.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the inequalities $c_i^2\leq c_{i-1}c_{i+1}$ fail for
every $i=1,2,3$, even for modules of the form $IF$ and $JF$
with $I,J$ $\mathfrak m$-primary.}

label: ex:failure-minkowski-modules
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:failure-minkowski-modules}
{\rm The following example shows that both the inequalities
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N\right)
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[i]},E_2^{[q-i]};N\right)
\leq e_{\rm BR}(E_1;N)e_{\rm BR}(E_2;N)
\]
and
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;N)^{1/q}
\leq e_{\rm BR}(E_1;N)^{1/q}
   +e_{\rm BR}(E_2;N)^{1/q},
\qquad q=d+p-1,
\]
can fail, even over a regular local ring of dimension three.

Let $R=k[[x,y,z]]$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m=(x,y,z)$,
and set
\(
F=R^2,\,\, N=R,\,\,
E_1=\mathfrak mF,\,\, E_2=\mathfrak m^2F.
\)
Both modules have finite colength in $F$, and $q=4$.
Writing $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)=R[t_1,t_2]$, we obtain
\(
E_1^{n_1}E_2^{n_2}
=\mathfrak m^{n_1+2n_2}S_{n_1+n_2}.
\)
Therefore,
\[
h_R(n_1,n_2;R)
=(n_1+n_2+1)\binom{n_1+2n_2+2}{3},
\]
whose homogeneous component of degree four is
\[
[h_R]_4
=\frac{
n_1^4+7n_1^3n_2+18n_1^2n_2^2
+20n_1n_2^3+8n_2^4}{6}.
\]
Setting
\[
e_i=e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[4-i]},E_2^{[i]};R\right),
\qquad 0\leq i\leq4,
\]
and comparing coefficients with
$\sum_{i=0}^4 e_i n_1^{4-i}n_2^i/((4-i)!\,i!)$ gives
\[
(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)=(4,7,12,20,32).
\]
In particular,
\[
e_1e_3=140>128=e_0e_4,
\qquad
e_2^2=144>128=e_0e_4.
\]
Thus the first proposed inequality fails for every
$i=1,2,3$.

Moreover, the product formula yields
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;R)
=\sum_{i=0}^{4}\binom4i e_i
=4+28+72+80+32
=216.
\]
By the strict concavity of $t\mapsto t^{3/4}$,
\[
\frac{1+2^{3/4}}2
<
\left(\frac32\right)^{3/4}.
\]
Hence
\[
\left(4^{1/4}+32^{1/4}\right)^4
=4\left(1+2^{3/4}\right)^4
<64\left(\frac32\right)^3
=216.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;R)^{1/4}
>
e_{\rm BR}(E_1;R)^{1/4}
+e_{\rm BR}(E_2;R)^{1/4},
\]
which disproves the proposed Minkowski-type inequality.}

label: prop:root-equality-criterion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:root-equality-criterion}
Let $E_1,E_2\subsetneq F$ have finite colength.
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)]
All mixed multiplicities
$e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]})$ are positive,
and there exist positive integers $r,s$ such that
\[
\frac{
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
}{
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i+1]},E_2^{[i-1]}\right)
}
=\frac rs
\qquad(1\leq i\leq q).
\]
\item[(b)]
For every $0\leq i\leq q$,
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
=
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}
e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Either condition implies
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)^{1/q}
=
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}+e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{1/q}.
\]
Conversely, if
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
\leq
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}
e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q}
\qquad(1\leq i\leq q-1),
\]
then this equality implies conditions \textup{(a)} and
\textup{(b)}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose \textup{(a)} holds. Iterating the ratio identities gives
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)\left(\frac rs\right)^i
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q).
\]
Taking $i=q$, we obtain
\[
e_{\rm BR}(E_2)
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)\left(\frac rs\right)^q.
\]
Since $r/s>0$ and $e_{\rm BR}(E_1)>0$, it follows that
\[
\frac rs
=
\left(\frac{e_{\rm BR}(E_2)}{e_{\rm BR}(E_1)}\right)^{1/q}.
\]
Substituting this expression into the first identity yields,
for every $0\leq i\leq q$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
&=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)
\left(\frac{e_{\rm BR}(E_2)}{e_{\rm BR}(E_1)}\right)^{i/q}\\
&=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}
  e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q},
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves \textup{(b)}.

Conversely, suppose \textup{(b)} holds. Since
$e_{\rm BR}(E_1)$ and $e_{\rm BR}(E_2)$ are positive,
all the mixed multiplicities are positive. Moreover, for
$1\leq i\leq q$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
}{
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i+1]},E_2^{[i-1]}\right)
}
&=
\frac{
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q}
}{
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i+1)/q}e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{(i-1)/q}
}\\
&=
\left(\frac{e_{\rm BR}(E_2)}{e_{\rm BR}(E_1)}\right)^{1/q}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus all consecutive ratios coincide. Taking $i=1$ shows
that their common value is
\(
\frac{
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-1]},E_2^{[1]}\right)
}{
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)
}.
\) As both the numerator and the denominator are positive
integers, this value can be written as $r/s$ with
$r,s\geq1$, proving \textup{(a)}.

We next prove the asserted equality. Under \textup{(b)},
Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-product-formula} and the binomial theorem give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}
e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q}\\
&=\left(
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}
+e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{1/q}
\right)^q.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking $q$-th roots yields the desired conclusion.

Finally, assume that the additional coefficient bounds
hold and that
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)^{1/q}
=
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}+e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{1/q}.
\]
Raising both sides to the $q$-th power and applying
Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-product-formula} and the binomial theorem, we obtain
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
\left[
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{(q-i)/q}
e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{i/q}
-
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
\right]=0.
\]
The bracketed expressions vanish for $i=0,q$ and are
nonnegative for $1\leq i\leq q-1$ by assumption.
Since every binomial coefficient is positive, each
bracketed expression must vanish. This proves
\textup{(b)}, and hence also \textup{(a)}.

label: prop:general-minkowski-br
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The ideals $I_1,I_2$ are $\mathfrak m$-primary and satisfy
$I_jF\subseteq E_j$. Hence, writing
$S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$, we obtain
\[
(I_1^rI_2^s)^nS_{(r+s)n}
\subseteq E_1^{rn}E_2^{sn}.
\]
By right exactness of tensor products,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\ell_R\!\left(
(S_{(r+s)n}/E_1^{rn}E_2^{sn})\otimes_RN
\right)\leq
\binom{(r+s)n+p-1}{p-1}
\ell_R\!\left(N/(I_1^rI_2^s)^nN\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying by $q!/n^q$ and taking limits yields
\[
\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^rE_2^s;N)
\leq
\binom qd(r+s)^{p-1}e(I_1^rI_2^s;N).
\]
The product formula of Corollary~\ref{mixed} gives
\[
\widetilde e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^rE_2^s;N)
=
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\mathrm{BR}}(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)
r^{q-i}s^i,
\]
proving the first inequality.

For the second inequality, apply Minkowski's inequality
for ideals with coefficients in $N$:
\[
e(I_1^rI_2^s;N)^{1/d}
\leq
r\,e(I_1;N)^{1/d}+s\,e(I_2;N)^{1/d}.
\]
For completeness, this module version follows from the
classical inequality \cite{RS,Verma}, associativity, and
H\"older's inequality. Indeed, let
\[
\Lambda=\{\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Supp}_RN:
                 \dim(R/\mathfrak p)=d\},
\qquad
w_{\mathfrak p}=\ell_{R_{\mathfrak p}}(N_{\mathfrak p}),
\]
and put $a_{\mathfrak p}=e(I_1;R/\mathfrak p)^{1/d}$
and $b_{\mathfrak p}=e(I_2;R/\mathfrak p)^{1/d}$.
Associativity and the classical inequality give
\[
e(I_1^rI_2^s;N)^{1/d}
\leq
\left(
\sum_{\mathfrak p\in\Lambda}
w_{\mathfrak p}(ra_{\mathfrak p}+sb_{\mathfrak p})^d
\right)^{1/d}.
\]
The weighted $\ell^d$ triangle inequality bounds this by
\[
r\left(\sum_{\mathfrak p\in\Lambda}
w_{\mathfrak p}a_{\mathfrak p}^d\right)^{1/d}
+
s\left(\sum_{\mathfrak p\in\Lambda}
w_{\mathfrak p}b_{\mathfrak p}^d\right)^{1/d}
=
r\,e(I_1;N)^{1/d}+s\,e(I_2;N)^{1/d}.
\]
This proves the second inequality.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
For $p=1$, Proposition~\ref{prop:general-minkowski-br}
recovers the classical Minkowski inequality for ideals.
Indeed, identify $F$ with $R$. Then $E_1,E_2$ are
$\mathfrak m$-primary ideals,
$I_j=(E_j:_RR)=E_j$, and $q=d$.
Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities become Hilbert--Samuel
multiplicities, so the proposition gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{d}\binom di
e(E_1^{[d-i]},E_2^{[i]};N)r^{d-i}s^i
\leq
\left(
r\,e(E_1;N)^{1/d}
+s\,e(E_2;N)^{1/d}
\right)^d.
\]
By the product formula for mixed multiplicities, the
left-hand side equals $e(E_1^rE_2^s;N)$. Therefore
\[
e(E_1^rE_2^s;N)^{1/d}
\leq
r\,e(E_1;N)^{1/d}+s\,e(E_2;N)^{1/d}.
\]
Taking $r=s=1$ yields
\[
e(E_1E_2;N)^{1/d}
\leq e(E_1;N)^{1/d}+e(E_2;N)^{1/d},
\]
which, for $N=R$, is the classical Minkowski inequality.

label: prop_br_bounds
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop_br_bounds}
Let $E_1,E_2\subseteq F$ have finite colength.
Set $K=E_1\cap E_2$. Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;N)
&=
\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom{q}{i}
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]};N\right)\\
&\leq 2^q e_{\rm BR}(K;N).
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, if $E_1\subseteq E_2$ or $E_2\subseteq E_1$,
then
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;N)
\leq
2^q\max\{e_{\rm BR}(E_1;N),e_{\rm BR}(E_2;N)\}.
\]
Equality holds in both estimates when $E_1=E_2$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$.
The natural injection \(
F/K\longrightarrow F/E_1\oplus F/E_2
\)
shows that $K$ has finite colength in $F$. Since $K\subseteq E_1$ and $K\subseteq E_2$, for every
$n\geq1$ we have
\[
K^{2n}\subseteq E_1^nE_2^n=(E_1E_2)^n
\subseteq S_{2n}.
\]
Thus there is a surjection
\[
(S_{2n}/K^{2n})\otimes_R N
\twoheadrightarrow
(S_{2n}/E_1^nE_2^n)\otimes_R N.
\]
Taking lengths, multiplying by $q!/n^q$, and passing to
the limit yields
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2;N)
\leq 2^q e_{\rm BR}(K;N).
\]
The expression in terms of mixed multiplicities follows
from Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-product-formula}.

If $E_1\subseteq E_2$, then $K=E_1$.
Moreover, the surjections
\[
(S_n/E_1^n)\otimes_R N
\twoheadrightarrow
(S_n/E_2^n)\otimes_R N
\]
give $e_{\rm BR}(E_1;N)\geq e_{\rm BR}(E_2;N)$.
Hence the asserted bound by the maximum follows.
The other inclusion is treated symmetrically.

Finally, if $E_1=E_2=E$, then $K=E$ and
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E^2;N)
=2^q e_{\rm BR}(E;N),
\]
which proves the equality assertion.

label: prop:equal-closures-mixed-equalities
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:equal-closures-mixed-equalities}
Let $E_1,E_2\subsetneq F$ have finite colength and assume that they have the
same integral closure in $F$. Then 
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)=e_{\rm BR}(E_2)
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q).
\]
Moreover, regarding $E_1E_2$ as a submodule of
$\operatorname{Sym}_R^2(F)$, one has
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)
=2^q e_{\rm BR}(E_1).
\]
In particular, the Minkowski-type equality holds:
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)^{1/q}
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}+e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{1/q}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H=\overline{E_1}=\overline{E_2}\subseteq F$.
Since $H$ is a submodule of the finite module $F$ over
the Noetherian ring $R$, it is finitely generated.
The inclusion $E_1\subseteq H$ induces a surjection
$F/E_1\twoheadrightarrow F/H$, so $H$ has finite colength.
Furthermore, $E_j\subseteq H=\overline{E_j}$ for $j=1,2$;
and the reduction criterion in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} then shows that both $E_1$ and $E_2$ are reductions of $H$.

By invariance under reductions
(Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-br-basic-properties}\textup{(iii)}) and the formula for
repeated modules (Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-br-basic-properties}\textup{(ii)}), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
&=e_{\rm BR}\left(H^{[q-i]},H^{[i]}\right)\\
&=e_{\rm BR}(H)
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q).
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking $i=0$ and $i=q$ gives
\[
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)=e_{\rm BR}(H)=e_{\rm BR}(E_2),
\]
which proves the first assertion.

Now Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-product-formula} and the binomial identity give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)\\
&=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)\sum_{i=0}^{q}\binom qi\\
&=2^q e_{\rm BR}(E_1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking $q$-th roots and using
$e_{\rm BR}(E_1)=e_{\rm BR}(E_2)$ yields
\[
\widetilde e_{\rm BR}(E_1E_2)^{1/q}
=2e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)^{1/q}+e_{\rm BR}(E_2)^{1/q}.
\]

label: ex:mixed-br-equality-distinct-closures
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:mixed-br-equality-distinct-closures}
{\rm Equality of all mixed Buchsbaum--Rim multiplicities does
not imply equality of integral closures, even over a
complete, reduced, Cohen--Macaulay local ring.

Let $k$ be an infinite field and set
\(
R=k[[x,y]]/(xy),\,\, \mathfrak m=(x,y),
\)
where $x,y$ also denote their residue classes in $R$.
The ring $R$ is complete, reduced, Cohen--Macaulay, and
equidimensional of dimension one; in particular, it is
quasi-unmixed. Consider
\[
I=(x,y^2),\qquad J=(x^2,y),\qquad
F=Rf_1\oplus Rf_2,
\]
and set $E_1=IF$ and $E_2=JF$.
Both modules have finite colength in $F$, and
$q=\dim R+\operatorname{rank}F-1=2$.

For integers $a,b\geq1$, the relation $xy=0$ gives
\(
I^aJ^b=(x^{a+2b},y^{2a+b}).
\)
Since
\[
\ell_R\bigl(R/(x^u,y^v)\bigr)=u+v-1
\qquad(u,v\geq1),
\]
we obtain $\ell_R(R/I^aJ^b)=3(a+b)-1$.
Writing $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)=R[t_1,t_2]$, we have
\[
E_1^aE_2^b=I^aJ^bS_{a+b}.
\]
The module $S_{a+b}$ is free of rank $a+b+1$, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_R(S_{a+b}/E_1^aE_2^b)
&=(a+b+1)\ell_R(R/I^aJ^b)\\
&=(a+b+1)\bigl(3(a+b)-1\bigr)\\
&=3a^2+6ab+3b^2+2a+2b-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing its quadratic terms with
\[
\frac{e_{\rm BR}(E_1)}{2}a^2
+e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[1]})ab
+\frac{e_{\rm BR}(E_2)}{2}b^2
\]
yields
\[
e_{\rm BR}(E_1)
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1^{[1]},E_2^{[1]})
=e_{\rm BR}(E_2)=6.
\]

Nevertheless, $\overline{E_1}\neq\overline{E_2}$ in $F$.
Indeed, $xf_1\in E_1$. Suppose that
$xf_1\in\overline{E_2}$. Identifying $f_1,f_2$ with
$t_1,t_2$, respectively, there would exist an equation
\[
(xt_1)^n+a_1(xt_1)^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n=0,
\qquad a_j\in E_2^j,
\]
for some $n\geq1$.
Apply the homomorphism
\[
\varphi:R[t_1,t_2]\longrightarrow k[[x]],
\qquad
x\longmapsto x,\quad y\longmapsto0,\quad
t_1\longmapsto1,\quad t_2\longmapsto0.
\]
Since $\varphi(E_2)\subseteq(x^2)$, this gives
\[
x^n+\varphi(a_1)x^{n-1}+\cdots+\varphi(a_n)=0,
\qquad \varphi(a_j)\in(x^{2j}).
\]
Thus $x$ would be integral over $(x^2)$ in the discrete
valuation ring $k[[x]]$. This is impossible because
$(x^2)$ is integrally closed and $x\notin(x^2)$.
Therefore
\(
xf_1\in\overline{E_1}\setminus\overline{E_2}.
\)
This disproves the implication
\textup{(i)}$\Rightarrow$\textup{(ii)}
in Question~\ref{converse}.}

label: prop:converse-scalar-integral-closures
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:converse-scalar-integral-closures}
Assume in addition that $R$ is quasi-unmixed and $d\geq2$.
Let $E_1,E_2\subsetneq F$ be submodules of finite colength.
Assume that there exist $\mathfrak m$-primary ideals $I,J$
such that
\(
\overline{E_1}=\overline{IF}
\,\,\text{and}\,\,
\overline{E_2}=\overline{JF},
\)
where integral closures are taken in $F$.
Then the following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}]
For every $0\leq i\leq q$,
\(
e_{\rm BR}\left(E_1^{[q-i]},E_2^{[i]}\right)
=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)=e_{\rm BR}(E_2).
\)
\item[\textup{(ii)}]
$\overline{E_1}=\overline{E_2}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, this equivalence holds when $E_1=IF$
and $E_2=JF$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The implication \textup{(ii)} $\Rightarrow$ \textup{(i)}
follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:equal-closures-mixed-equalities}.

Conversely, assume \textup{(i)}, and write
$A=e_{\rm BR}(E_1)=e_{\rm BR}(E_2)$.
By invariance under integral closure,
\[
e_{\rm BR}\left((IF)^{[q-i]},(JF)^{[i]}\right)=A
\qquad(0\leq i\leq q).
\]
Let $S=\operatorname{Sym}_R(F)$. Since
\(
(IF)^a(JF)^b=I^aJ^bS_{a+b},
\)
we have
\[
\ell_R\left(S_{a+b}/(IF)^a(JF)^b\right)
=
\binom{a+b+p-1}{p-1}\ell_R(R/I^aJ^b).
\]
Comparing the homogeneous components of total degree $q$
in the corresponding Hilbert polynomials gives
\[
\frac{A}{q!}(X+Y)^q
=
\frac{(X+Y)^{p-1}}{(p-1)!\,d!}
\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom dj
e\left(I^{[d-j]},J^{[j]}\right)X^{d-j}Y^j.
\]
Canceling $(X+Y)^{p-1}$ and comparing coefficients, we obtain
\[
e\left(I^{[d-j]},J^{[j]}\right)
=\frac{A}{\binom qd}
=e(I)=e(J)
\qquad(0\leq j\leq d).
\]
In particular,
\[
e(IJ)=2^d e(I),
\]
and hence
\[
e(IJ)^{1/d}=e(I)^{1/d}+e(J)^{1/d}.
\]
Since $R$ is quasi-unmixed and $d\geq2$, the equality
criterion in \cite[Theorem~1.16]{Verma} yields positive
integers $r,s$ such that
$\overline{I^r}=\overline{J^s}$.
Taking multiplicities gives
\(
r^d e(I)=s^d e(J).
\)
Thus $r=s$, and consequently $\overline I=\overline J$.

To pass to modules, set $H=I+J$. The equality
$\overline I=\overline J$ implies that both $I$ and $J$
are reductions of $H$. If $H^{n+1}=IH^n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$, then
\[
(HF)^{n+1}
=H^{n+1}S_{n+1}
=IH^nS_{n+1}
=(IF)(HF)^n.
\]
Therefore, $IF$ is a reduction of $HF$; likewise, $JF$
is a reduction of $HF$. It follows that
\[
\overline{E_1}
=\overline{IF}
=\overline{HF}
=\overline{JF}
=\overline{E_2},
\]
as required.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The hypothesis on the integral closures includes modules
that are not themselves of the form $IF$. For example,
the proposition applies whenever $E_1$ and $E_2$ are
reductions of $IF$ and $JF$, respectively.
No assumption on the cardinality of the residue field
is needed.
